'in quibusdam res ipsa declaravit' is ambiguous; it may mean the doubt was later shown in certain others. A stray footnote numeral after 'ignis' was omitted. The heading of Chapter II stands at the end of this line in the edition and is kept there. 1.1.6: the closing words of Severus' letter are odd ('in salutem omnium illic credentium ... Judæorum'); taken as the conversion of the Jews of Minorca.

Line 8: 'Jesu' refers to Joshua (Latin Jesus Nave), Moses' general against Amalek in Exod. 17. 'infantis villici' is uncertain; it may be a proper name (e.g. 'Infans the bailiff'). 'parvulorum (??)iorum' read as 'parvulorum filiorum'. Line 10: 'an aritudine' read as 'amaritudine'. Line 12: 'in ligata' read as 'instigata'. Memplonitanum is an unidentified place. 'Memoria' is rendered 'shrine' (the martyr's memorial chapel). In the Dativus story, 'reddere' Symbolum means reciting back the Creed, as catechumens did.

Promontorium (the 'Promontoriensis ecclesia'), Pisita and the Zarites ('Zaritorum') in the territory of Hippo could not be securely identified. In the Rusticanus chapter, 'Uzalensis' is apparently both the leading citizen's name and the word for 'man of Uzalis'; Stephen plays on this. 'Die Romanorum civitatis' is obscure; it is perhaps a local festival or a market day. 'Folles' are small bronze coins. The opening 'Ubi' of the Rusticanus chapter seems to have been carried over from the heading formula; I have rendered it as 'When'.

1.31: 'in(??)nitis' read as 'infinitis', 'poten(??)' as 'potentiae'. 2.2: the opening sentence is anacoluthic (the stray 'cum' and an implied 'est' with 'exhibitum'); translated by sense. 'oculata fide' rendered 'eye-witnessed faith'. 'cum clausula sua' (with their closing passage) is uncertain in sense. 2.4: 'Fro(??)s' read as 'Frons'; '(??)ater' read as 'pater'; heading 'fuera' read as 'fuerat'. The sentence 'Cæterorum namque membrorum ... subtrahuntur' is compressed and translated by sense.

Line 2.5: 'Diei non potest' read as 'Dici non potest'. 'a corona tua' ('from your crown') is obscure; perhaps the martyr's shrine or the assembly gathered there. 'lumina' in 'octavi mensis... tremenda lumina' taken as 'days'. Line 2.7: Pontius' dream words 'posuisse jam jugulos' ('I have laid down my necks') are odd; Vitula's gloss links them to the 'yoke' (jugum) of Christ, so a pun or corruption of 'jugum' may lie behind them. 'mane facta oratione' read with 'facta' as an intrusion or footnote mark. The parenthesis on Pontius' conversion leaves the main sentence (begun 'Flexis itaque illis...') without a conclusion; the narrative resumes in 2.8. Line 2.8: the scripture citation is damaged in the scan ('in P(??) (??)ant', 'die a(??) dicitur', reference missing); restored as Ps. 41:4 ('in Psalmis cantant', 'die ac nocte, dum dicitur').

2.9: the sentence on the 'eyes' is damaged in the scan; read as 'curandi, non utique corporis, sed cordis, quod, ut [verus] medicus, ... pronuntiavit [dicens: Pr]ius', the bracketed words being conjectural. 'quasi cutem medicinalem collyrium imposuit' is awkward and may be corrupt; rendered loosely. 'visitavit in somnis' (2.12) taken as passive 'was visited'. 2.10: 'Infans' as a form of address to the virgin Helpidiana is unusual; rendered 'Child'. 'in obsequium' taken as 'to attend her' at the baths.

Line 2: '(??)gunculam' read as 'lagunculam' (small flask). 'cum loco et nomine vocitato' is obscure; rendered 'called by the name of its place'. 'non tam molestante damnum jactura' seems corrupt; rendered by sense. Line 4: the passage after the Psalm quotation is damaged; restorations such as 'Abyssus namque', 'aeris', 'nubes', and 'si' or 'ne' before 'sicut insipienter' are conjectural. Line 5: several sentences ('Namque illud... in vero', 'Concurrebat... batur', 'imaginis... exemplariorum', 'in mu...', 'ad homines quaedam') are badly damaged; only fragments are translated. 'Memblotutano' may be the same place as 'Memplonitanus locus' in the glossary, but it is kept as printed. 'conferentem caput' is read as 'conterentem' (crushing), as the picture describes.

Lines 2.21–2.26 are not part of the Miracles: they are the opening of the printed volume's index (Migne, PL vol. 41, Augustine's City of God), carried into the text by the scan, and are translated as given. In 2.19 'officium quod patebat' is read as 'quod parebat' ('which was obeying'); the following '1' is a footnote mark. 'fuga dudum recreato animo' is obscure and translated literally. 'occultata sede intendere se' is uncertain; it is rendered 'from a hidden seat he was attending to him'. 'Immittet angelus Domini' follows an Old Latin form of Ps. 33:8, where the Vulgate has 'castrametabitur'. In 2.20 'limine' seems corrupt (perhaps 'lumine', 'in light'); it is rendered '[on the] threshold'. '(1)' after 'evaserit' is a footnote mark.

This stretch is not from the De miraculis sancti Stephani: it is part of the table of chapter headings for Augustine's City of God, Books 1–2, evidently printed in the same volume and misfiled under this work, as were the preceding lines. Numbers at line ends are page or column references of the printed edition. Scanning gaps restored from evident sense: parcerent (VI), plerumque (VIII), etiamsi (XII), exemplum and passa (XV, XVI), poenae (XVII), quam in (XVIII), quolibet (XX), sola (Book 2 summary), disputatione (XXXVI); licent read as licet (XXVI); obcresceret taken as increbresceret, 'spread' (II.III).

nodes.text: ON THE MIRACLES OF SAINT STEPHEN THE PROTOMARTYR
Two books.
BOOK ONE.

The record of the divine works which were shown through the venerable merit of the blessed protomartyr Stephen, and were also committed to the knowledge of the faithful by Evodius in the Church of Uzalis, a most worthy priest who was administering the episcopate of that city, while Aurelius Augustine was at that time established at Hippo as steward of the Lord's sowing.
Prologue.

Since the holy angel Raphael deigns to exhort us not so much to set the works of God away in hiding, as rather to lay them open for the glory of God, warning and saying, It is good to hide the secret of a king, but it is honourable to reveal and confess the works of God (Tob. 12:7); and since, just as it is unbelief not to give faith to things known, so it is envy to be unwilling to proclaim things known for the edification of others: for this reason, most blessed father Evodius, I have taken care to obey the commands of Your Paternity diligently, trusting not so much in my own strength as aided by the grace of God and by your holy prayers; so that the things which Christ has worked among us through our patron Stephen, his first martyr, and still deigns to work, I might not suppress by a spiteful silence, by which others would be cheated, but rather narrate with pious devotion, so that the glory of the Friend of God may be made known to the ears of the brethren: not as though we were able to magnify anything by talent or by any eloquence, but desiring to set out faithfully the truth of the facts themselves, as God has granted, so that our narration itself may not dare to seek a display of words, but rather strive to avoid the paint of lies; so that wherever the matter demands, we ought not to be ashamed to set down simply also the words of the people themselves, just as they were spoken by them. For to good and religious people whatever is said truly, even in faulty words, is more pleasing than falsehoods in polished and ornate words. Certainly, let no one think that we wished to narrate these things for this reason, as though we seemed to be offering some glory to the blessed Martyr: since we can neither take anything from him by keeping silent, nor confer anything by speaking. For the miracles of his mighty works themselves need no proclamation by the human tongue; they already sound forth a trumpet resounding everywhere: but we wish only to show our devotion with humility, for the edification of the brethren, so as to receive the reward of obedience, fearing also what we read was said terribly by the Lord himself, If you are silent, the stones will cry out (Luke 19:40). And I beg all of you, as many as wish to hear or read these things piously and religiously, that you deign always to remember in your holy prayers this last of sinners, who wrote this in the name of the Lord: and if anything is set forth by us in a rustic manner, do not be indignant; but only take delight, because it is said truthfully.
CHAPTER ONE. — On the flask of blood shown in a dream to a handmaid of God.

So, when there could not yet have been even a rumour that relics of the lord Saint Stephen, the first confessor of Christ in martyrdom, were to come to us unworthy ones (for we neither had it in our thoughts that this could happen, nor could we suspect it), behold, from an earlier time that glorious one began to reveal himself to certain holy souls among us. For when in a certain place or on a certain day there was talk of the aforesaid relics among those servants of God who had them, sent to them from the regions of the East without our knowing, there was present at the conversation also a certain woman, a consecrated handmaid of God; who, when she heard this, as tends to happen, did not readily believe, and began to say silently within herself: And who knows whether they really are relics of martyrs? But immediately on the following night a certain flask was shown to her in a dream, holding within it a certain sprinkling of blood and, as it were, a token of bones in the form of ears of grain; holding this in his hand a certain priest spoke to her brother, a monk, in her presence, saying: Do you want to know how relics of martyrs are proved? With these words he thrust the flask into his mouth, and at once a flame of fire began to pour out through his ears and eyes. Kindly hear how this was made manifest in reality. The flask, just as the handmaid of God saw it with her eyes in the revelation of the dream, so afterwards the priest of God received it into his hands in the manifestation of the thing itself; and the doubt she had earlier had within herself, the thing itself has now shown up in certain people. Then, that the fire seized the ears and eyes through the flask, what else did it foreshadow then, but that the proclamation of the holy relics, reaching the mouth of the monks, set alight the one body of the Church with the fire of God's brightness through hearing and sight, so that all might rightly say, As we have heard, so also have we seen (Ps. 47:9)? Nor was it idle that that priest appeared who applied the flask, which gave out fire, to the monk's mouth. For he was the one who, lately returning from the East and putting into the mouths of the servants of God an account of the holy relics he had seen there, as it were brought the flask to them and set them alight with holy fire. But I would now wish to pass on to the clearer and more evident miracles of our patron Stephen, if I did not think it relevant to set before Your Holiness yet another vision. I ask that you deign to hear it patiently and, as I think, not fruitlessly. CHAPTER II. — Where Saint Stephen appeared to a virgin.

Another consecrated virgin seemed to herself in a dream to be making her way to the shrine of the ancient martyrs established in the suburb of the city, who are called Felix and Gennadius, not by the road by which one usually goes from the city by the short way, but by one somewhat out of the way and winding. Along this she sees countless crowds approaching, rejoicing indeed and singing psalms, and carrying candles and lamps with great festivity, and as it were escorting a certain little one clothed in white, and crying out to him with repeated voices: Confessor of Christ, confessor of Christ. When they had brought him to the church and lifted him up onto the pulpit, she sees that same little one suddenly stretch out his hands and say to the people with his mouth close to them: Behold, you have a martyr. It is wonderful to tell how great a truth followed this vision too: and not without reason was it once foretold by a divine voice through the prophet: Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will give of my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters will prophesy, and young men will see visions, and old men will dream dreams: and upon my servants and my handmaids I will pour out of my Spirit: and I will give signs in heaven above and on earth below (Joel 2:28-30). Hence too a star is reported to have appeared at the shrine of the aforesaid martyrs, by those who were then in the countryside. Now, if you please, let us begin to show the fruit of the second vision. So, about forty days after these things were revealed, at the shrine of our martyrs mentioned above, to which she had seen herself going, having received the relics there and celebrated the sacraments of the faithful, we began to return from there to the city, singing and chanting psalms with the choirs of an immense multitude; and along that very road which had been shown to the girl the holy relics were carried in a vehicle, in the lap of the holy bishop seated in it, like that little one in white who had been seen by her. For in the portion of his body that little one is recognised as the confessor of Christ. Do you doubt whether the martyr is a little one? Is he not an infant because of his innocence, and small because of his humility? Finally, the very hymn that was sung by the mouth of all the people, that is, Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord (Ps. 117:26), what else is it understood to have signified, while it was sung with repeated voice, but what was said in her hearing, Confessor of Christ, confessor of Christ? And indeed, just as had been shown to the girl, so they shone with candles and lamps. And we too entered the same church which she had seen in the vision. One last thing of the whole vision now remains: that the girl had seen that confessor lifted onto the pulpit, and had heard him, with hands outstretched, saying to the people, Behold, you have a martyr. Deign to hear how this too was fulfilled at the proper time by divine provision. For on the same day on which the relics of blessed Stephen entered the church, at the very beginning of the canonical readings, a letter of a certain holy bishop named Severus, of the island of Minorca, which had been brought to us also, was read out from the pulpit to the ears of the Church with great acclaim: it contained the mighty works of the glorious Stephen which he had accomplished in the said island through the presence of his relics, for the salvation of all the Jews there who believed. Hence, through this reading of such deeds of his, as by the stretching out of his hands, while the faithful acclaimed and rejoiced, he himself seemed to say, Behold, you have a martyr. But let these things have been said so that we might in some way commend to the brethren how the relics of Saint Stephen appear to have come to us, however sinful we are as men, not by chance or at random, but by divine favour.
CHAPTER III. — On the blind woman who touched the cloth over the relics and recovered her sight.

Now therefore, as we promised, let us come to better-known miracles. When, then, on the evening of that same day, the relics had been placed in the area of the apse upon the veiled throne, a certain woman named Hilara, deprived of her eyes, a breadseller known to the citizens, stirred by faith in the great glory of the Martyr and wavering with no doubt of unbelief (He who hesitates, says the apostle James, will be likened to a wave of the sea, which is moved and driven about by the wind [James 1:6]): this woman, then, strengthened in faith, made firm in the hope of receiving light, and inflamed with love of divine grace, [made for] the place where the relics were, which she could not approach in body by herself, since her eyes of flesh hindered her, but which she had already reached in spirit with the shining eyes of the heart; she asked a certain devout woman to give her a hand and lead her to the place from which she trusted she would receive light. When she had been led there by the help of another's hand, she grasped with a groping hand the cloth laid over the relics, and at once applied it to both her eyes; and she went away from there not yet indeed enlightened in body, but already irradiated with the light of faith. For, praying now with her mouth, now with her heart, she did not keep silent the name of the glorious Martyr, nor that of Christ the Lord. When she had been led back to her house, there too, within her own walls, she fought with continual prayer to overcome the darkness of blindness, as Joshua [fought] against the enemy Amalek (Exod. 17). Only a little of the night had passed, when behold, the woman, going out over the threshold of her door, little by little began to recover light, so that she saw the walls opposite and made out the paving stones of the street. At once she called her son and began to address him with these words: Son, aren't those the walls of the house of the bailiff's child? Look, and the paving stones of the street. And her son said to her: Why are you lying? thinking that she said it to test him, not because she saw. Again lifting her eyes to the sky, she said: Look, I see the moon too over the theatre, still at half. And her son said to her: Why did you pretend not to see? as though his mother had never before been blind, but had rather feigned blindness. No wonder if the natural man did not yet perceive the things of the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2:14), not knowing what had been foretold long ago: Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened (Isa. 35:5). But she, not conscious of a feigned former blindness, as her son thought, but conscious of new light received, as the truth was, gave thanks to the Friend of Christ: for not in vain had she sung to God, You will light my lamp, O Lord my God, you will light up my darkness (Ps. 17:32); and, You give light wonderfully from the everlasting mountains (Ps. 75:5): she was thus heard and enlightened from the everlasting mountains. Next day in the morning she went to the church alone, with no one accompanying her, but led by her own sight; she did not hide the praises of God and of the Friend of God, and she recounted what had been wonderfully done in her, while the faithful congratulated her and marvelled. This, then, was the first [miracle] known among us at the coming of the holy relics.
CHAPTER IV. — On the man who had broken his foot in a fall and was made whole; and on the many who were cured of various diseases.

About the same time a certain barber of the city, who was called Concordius, had broken his foot in a fall. Lying in bed a long time, he was tormented by various pains. While on the one hand the thought of poverty, on the other the care of his little children wore him down, placed as he was in such grief at his misfortune, behold, one night, while he himself was asleep, but He was not slumbering or sleeping who keeps Israel (Ps. 120:4), who made small and great, and has care for all alike (Wisd. 6:8), he sees in a dream that he has been led up a steep and narrow ascent of a certain mountain, from which he had no means of returning, no way out to escape. What else was shown by this, than that he should know and understand that in the straits of his troubles he ought to seek not human help, but that of God alone? For he said that there appeared to him a certain woman of venerable aspect, who, as he was so afflicted and filled with the bitterness of pains, handed him what looked like a fig, through the meaning of whose sweetness he was to perceive the delight of spiritual grace. Hence, gaining confidence of obtaining [his request], he persisted in prayers and asked health of her. But she, who without doubt bore a figure of the Church, said: Go now to Saint Stephen, and he will make you well. The fulfilment of the deed followed this saying. For as she was leaving, and he, grieving to be left behind her, said, Are you leaving me and taking yourself off? behold, he sees her, as she had promised him, going to Saint Stephen and asking on his behalf, saying in these words: I ask you by your holiness, heal him; have mercy on him, have mercy on his children, free an innocent man from tribulation. Then he saw the one who was being asked coming in to him and to the bedroom in which he lay, clothed in a white garment, comely in appearance. As soon as he recognised him, like a sick man his physician, a needy man a rich one, a suppliant his patron, he begged him with tears in these words, saying: Dear friend of Christ, heal me, free me from tribulation, have mercy on me, have mercy on my children. Scarcely had the petitioner finished his words, and already the hearer of prayers was answering the prayers, saying: Rise, you have been made whole. And he at once, at the word of the one commanding, as one who had heard while sleeping in body but awake in spirit, immediately leapt from the bed and began to walk with firm steps in front of his bed, and so fulfilled that word of prophecy, And the lame man shall leap like a deer (Isa. 35:6). Then in the morning he rises and hastened to pay his vows to the Martyrs, where those same relics had been received. Because of the length of the journey he thought he should still lean on a staff. There, after he had prayed a long time, he lit candles, left the staff behind, and from there walked back carrying his little son on his neck: he came into the church and proclaimed the glory of God and of the Friend of God by the testimony of his health. After this, when the relics had been placed in the church with great solemnity, as though a station of healing had been set up (whence we sang, We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your temple [Ps. 47:10]), how great a crowd began from that day to flock together from every side, how many benefits have been bestowed and are bestowed daily, how many miracles shown, how many blind given light, paralytics healed, how many cured of various diseases and afflictions, and even the dead raised — it is long and almost impossible for us either to retain them all in memory, or to set them out in speech, or to commit them to writing; since each miracle is known to have a certain story of its own kind. Yet of all these, which we can neither unfold nor ought to pass over wholly in silence, we choose some of the fewer and better known, so that we neither flood the ears of the squeamish nor cheat the zeal of the diligent.
CHAPTER V. — On the woman who called on Saint Stephen for her husband, and was heard.

So a certain woman of the place Memplonitanum, whose husband had long been travelling abroad, being neither certain of his death nor assured of his life, when almost three years' time had passed, during which, harried by various rumours about her spouse, she had been set in a doubtful and uncertain state of life, her woman's mind wavered, hanging on uncertainty, and she did not know to which side to throw herself in her distress, while on one side marriage was urged on her, poverty set before her, anxiety pressed upon her, the frailty of the flesh lay in ambush; again, on the other side, chastity, her husband, reputation, religion were set before her eyes: at length, amid the surge of such conflicting thoughts, she was urged and encouraged by certain people, not without divine providence, that she ought to implore the patronage of the most powerful advocate Stephen. For she flew as a suppliant to his shrine, and there prostrated herself with tears. And while she prays, she was found worthy to hear, Your husband is coming. Quickly she went back home, and found her husband safe and sound. Thus both chastity was preserved for the wife, and it became known, in the wonderful grace of God, how great was the Friend of God's care for a soul in peril.
CHAPTER VI. — On the man whom a collapsing house had crushed, who, as his wife prayed to Saint Stephen, was found alive.

About the same time, in our city, a certain house falling in ruin had crushed a man whose name is Dativus. His body, dug out from there and carried to a neighbouring house, was being mourned with funeral rites. Accordingly his wife, struck by such grief for her husband, went to the shrine of the glorious Stephen to prostrate herself with tears for her husband's life. While she was there for some time knocking in faith at the ears of the Friend of God and persisting in prayers, behold, suddenly, in the sight of those mourning around the corpse and calling on the name of the venerable Martyr, her husband, in the place where he lay, began to open his eyes and move his body, while all who were present saw and marvelled: and then, after some part of that same day had passed, returning to the living and coming to himself, he said to the man whose house it was: You are blessed, brother, because today an angel of God has entered your house. And he began to tell what had been revealed to his soul. For he said that he had been surrounded by a multitude of the dead, some of whom he recognised, others not. Then a certain young man came in, shining in a white garment, wearing the dress of a deacon, and with a command of kindness ordering and saying to those dead, Withdraw; at once those crowds of the dead disappeared. Then he came up to him and said to him, Give back what you received. And when he did not understand, he repeated, Give back what you received. And a third time likewise he was commanded by him to give it back, and he answered, Do you bid me give back the Creed? And when he said, Give it back; he recited the Creed in order, and added, If you bid, I will recite the Lord's Prayer too: and at his nod he recited it. Then he signed the heart of the man lying there with the saving sign, and said to him: Rise now whole. And rising, as was said, he was made whole.
CHAPTER VII. — Where the saint forbade the bishop to presume to move his relics.

At the same time our venerable bishop had arranged to place some part of the same saint's relics in the church of Promontorium; the day on which this was to be done had also been fixed. Lo, about the third day before, two priests of our Church, of whom one, of riper age, Zumurus by name, is warned, as he himself afterwards related, to go to the bishop in the morning and tell him not to carry out what he had arranged to do with part of the relics. When the said priest had treated this carelessly and had not carried it to the bishop, a second time he is both severely rebuked and struck with a slap dealt to his face. The other priest, Donatus by name, related that in the very place of the shrine he saw our same bishop standing opposite him, carrying the sacraments, of snowy whiteness, in a cloth in his hands and about his neck. Addressing him at once, he said firmly: Put down here what you are carrying. And when another priest, standing at the bishop's left, said to him, And who else will carry it? he answered, What is that to you, so long as what the bishop is carrying is put back in its place? As it was revealed, so it was fulfilled after the third day. For when on the day before a carriage was already being made ready, so that the bishop might set out with part of the relics, suddenly, the report of this matter having spread through the city, an immense multitude streamed together to the church. A great uproar and clamour began to arise; zeal for the faith and love for the Friend of God inflamed everyone. The bishop is surrounded by pressing crowds, entreated and held fast, and not let go until, even with an oath interposed, he promised that he would take nothing of the relics out of the city: so that thus at last that storm of the people, raised by zeal for the faith, might be calmed, and at the same time the relics be gathered into one, and in the same place of the shrine where part of the relics had first been placed, there the other part likewise be laid. The priest Donatus seemed in a dream, as was said, to press the bishop carrying the sacraments, that is, bearing a portion of the sacred relics, to put back in its place what was being carried off by him. This was done, I believe, so that no occasion for division should be given, especially because this was taking place in the church which, first seized in the schism of the Donatists, was afterwards restored to Catholic unity, [as it remains] to this day. Hence too it took its name, so that it has deserved to be called the church Restituta.
CHAPTER VIII. On the blind man who touched the little casket of relics and received his sight.

Indeed, on the same day on which these things were being done, when that part of the relics, brought out from the dwelling of the monastery, was being carried to the church in the hands of the bishop with the great exultation of a festival and choirs of hymns resounding in sweet melody, lo, a certain blind man, laying hold of the little silver casket in which the said portion of the relics was, began with the strongest faith to do violence to the kingdom of heaven. And because those who do violence seize it (Matt. 11:12), he at once received light. By this Christ heaped no small joy upon his whole Church.
CHAPTER IX. — On two men in chains freed through the glorious Stephen.

Likewise, when certain men were being held in the public prison, bound rather strictly in chains, one of them, pierced by the torment of the punishment and by pain, called on Saint Stephen, dear to Christ, for help. And lo, amid the tears and cries of the man wailing, suddenly the chains fell from his hands. When this had happened, and, set free, he had of his own accord presented himself to the keeper of the prison and confessed the matter of so great a miracle, the keeper did not dare to put the fetters on him again, but, made clearly more cautious and anxious by this, he bound another prisoner more tightly and strongly: as if anything could be indissoluble to divine power, not knowing that the word of God is not bound (II Tim. 2:9). But when that man, driven by a like harshness of fetters, cried out as a suppliant to the same author of so great a miracle with such words and tears as his companion, he too was found worthy to be heard, and, his chains likewise loosed, he told of the works of God, confessing them.
CHAPTER X. — On a prisoner released and, through the merit of Saint Stephen, healed.

Likewise, when in another prisoner, in the public baths, the wounds from his chains swelled with the steam of the heat and roused very grievous pain in him, faith was at hand, so that he implored the help of the Friend of God. And when he had gone out to the pool, suddenly his chains too fell off, and all, as many as saw it, began to magnify Christ and his first confessor Stephen.
CHAPTER XI. — Where a paralytic was found worthy of health.

A paralytic of the territory of Hippo, of the Zarites, named Restitutus, a blacksmith, lying in bed for a very long time, could neither walk with his feet nor loosen his tongue into words: at length, when the fame of blessed Stephen reached him, he urged his own family, by such nods as he could, that he be carried to the shrine of the glorious martyr. When this was done, while he lay there in prayer for much of the winter, in such harshness of cold, on the tessellated pavement (which is certainly usually harmful to infirmities of this kind), about the twentieth day, he reported, there appeared to him at night in a dream someone of youthful form, handsome also in fine dress and bearing, and he was then summoned by him and commanded to come to the place of the shrine on his own feet: and from then he began little by little to recall his step and his tongue somewhat to their proper functions. And when the fourth month had passed, because he had not yet recovered full health, he began to think of returning home; and he says that he was then warned and told that he should not be in a hurry, but ought to wait four more months, at which time he would go back to his house on his own feet. This was fulfilled entirely as promised, on the day and at the time announced. For, as our own knowledge also bears witness, and as he himself confessed to the glory of God, he both returned home on his own feet and began to pronounce words more distinctly with his own mouth.
CHAPTER XII. Where a certain man was freed from paralysis of the tongue and feet.

A certain man of the city of Utica, afflicted with paralysis in his feet and tongue, was confined to bed. His mother flew with the firmest faith to the shrine of Saint Stephen, and, after she had entrusted her son's case to the best of advocates, took away with her from there some dust for sanctification, and, returning home, applied it to her son lying [in bed]. From this he soon, feeling the benefit of health, rose from his bed, and not only began to walk on his own feet, but even reached the shrine of the blessed martyr on foot over twelve miles, giving thanks in his heart for the health of his feet he had received, but still pouring out prayers for the loosing of his tongue. Accordingly, taking off the sleeve of his tunic, because he had no cloth, he would thrust it in with his hand through the little window of the shrine to the inner place of the holy relics, and then, drawing his right hand back again, he would bring it to his mouth, and by touching his tongue he gradually, by the grace of faith, loosed the knots of speech. For by doing this often, as if taking wholesome food from the heavenly storeroom, he applied it to his sick member: whereby he restored his parched tongue, and, helped by the grace of God, recovered the proper function of speech: and so in both was that prophecy fulfilled by which it was once said, And the tongue of the dumb shall be plain (Isa. 35:6).
CHAPTER XIII. — Where a blind man of Pisita received the light of his eyes.

Also a certain blind man of the city of Pisita, whose name is Donatianus, came to the station of the most powerful physician Stephen. There at length, knocking with the devotion of faith, on the eighth day, as in the mystery of the Lord's resurrection, which took place indeed on the third day from the passion, but in the count of days on the eighth after the sabbath, on that day, as I said, he received through faith the light of his eyes, on which the whole world received the light of minds through the Lord's Resurrection. When, wishing to pay his vows to the holy martyr, he offered a silver candle out of his devotion (and not without reason did he offer a candle who had received light), he was summoned by the venerable bishop and asked to tell him what had been granted him that he offered that gift; and, with the whole Church standing by, he confessed with his mouth too that he had been given back enlightened both in heart and body, the spiritual chief physician healing him. CHAPTER XIV. — Where Saint Stephen appeared to a man who had heard that his son had been killed by robbers.

When a butcher of our city named Rusticanus had sent his son, with another man of his, to buy pigs, with the solidi counted out, about two hundred miles away; and when several days had passed and they had not yet returned, he began to be blamed and reproached by a certain friend of his for having been willing to send his son and his man into so distant a region, who, he said, he had heard had already been killed by robbers. On hearing this, he, as if struck by pitiable grief, went back home weeping and mourning. He fed on tears instead of food the whole day. Meanwhile, when night had found him thus overwhelmed in the darkness of sorrow, lo, in a dream he sees appear to him a certain handsome young man, bearing the face and dress of an honourable and leading man of the city named Uzalensis, and [he sees] him say to him with a cheerful face: Why are you weeping? And he answered, to use his own simple words: My lord, by your goodness, I weep because I heard that my man and my son have been killed. But he, consoling him, said to him: They have not been killed. But who am I? he said. He answered: My lord Uzalensis. Well, he said, you have said that I am Uzalensis, but I am not the one you think: for I am Stephen. As for why you are sad about your son and your man, know that they already have their faces turned back here. For you gave them twenty-five solidi, and besides they received money on credit, nearly twenty thousand folles, and they are bringing with them pigs, forty-four in number, all choice ones. And they will come on the day of the city of the Romans, at the first hour. All these things, as they were revealed in the dream, so afterwards were fulfilled in fact. For the men returned safe, and the pigs were brought in that number, and the sum of the money on credit was found the same, and the day and hour of their arrival foretold came about without any error at all. CHAPTER XV. — On the little child who died a catechumen, and through the merits of Saint Stephen was restored alive to his mother.

1. A certain woman's little son had died a catechumen. Carried in his mother's hands, with huge wailing and pitiful outcry, he was laid down before the very shrine of the glorious Stephen, she handing him over dead so that she might receive him back from him alive. And while she knocked at the ears of the Friend of God with the faith of devotion, struck by a double grief of bereavement, because she had lost her son both in the present life and in the future one, since, being without the grace of Baptism, she could not have him saved, behold, amid the long-lamenting and crying-out grief and clamour of the wretched mother, suddenly breath is given back to the little one, life is bestowed, voice is granted to the living child. At once a priest is summoned, Baptism is given to the little one, the sacraments are completed, and so, his soul freed from the deadly chain of sins, he is immediately also stripped of the bond of mortal flesh and, set free, is sent off with the greatest speed to the spiritual embraces of God. Thus the mother, granted no small consolation, is allowed to rejoice over her son given back, and the little one is granted true salvation. He surely received life for a little while for this reason, that he might not die for eternity; for this reason he was found worthy to die for a time, that he might enjoy everlasting life.

2. These few, meanwhile, we have plucked from many and almost countless miracles, so as not perhaps to be a burden at present to the hearers who have come from far away for the Martyr's festival. Besides, what is most difficult for us, if we wished to recall and review all of them, as was said above, we would make a lengthy book. For we think that these most well-known and most celebrated mighty works suffice of themselves to proclaim themselves, needing no faculty of human tongue, since they prevail by the clear truth of divine power. Yet we wished to show our devotion in some part, in the name of Christ, for the edification of the brethren, so that we might receive the reward of filial obedience through your prayers and, with divine mercy favouring us, obtain the blessing of the glorious Stephen, the first witness of Christ: through Christ our Lord, to whom be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.
BOOK TWO.
CHAPTER ONE. — Address on a second book to be joined to the preceding one.

Your Holiness, most holy fathers and brothers, well recalls with me that when, in the assembly of this our Church of Uzalis, the miracles of the lord Stephen, first martyr of Christ, faithfully written down and proved by public attestation, were read out publicly before this time to you who were present, this gift too of fullest rejoicing was presented to your Charity, the Friend of God himself, as we believe, arranging it: that after the reading of the divine works and deeds, the clear showing and personal declaration of the very persons in whom those wonders were done, as many as could be found at the time, should not only bear witness to our writings, but also press the assurance of truth upon your eyes and sight. Hence it came about that, while these mighty works of God were first made known to your ears through the reading, they were also presented to your sight with eye-witnessed faith, so that what is written in the Psalm was fulfilled in you, As we have heard, so also have we seen (Ps. 47:9). For there was in so great a matter a grand spectacle of heavenly glory. For when the reader had pronounced any story, for example first about a certain blind woman afterwards given sight, at once, the reading ended, this same person was sought among the people, and found, and brought out into the midst of the whole Church, and to their wonder and rejoicing was seen now walking alone, without any companion or guide as she used to before; and she herself, climbing by herself the steps of the apse, stood to be seen from afar by all, and proclaimed the testimony of divine grace in herself by the very sight given to her eyes, as by a kind of silent preaching of faithful witnesses. Likewise, when the reading came first about the healed paralytic, known to many beforehand, at once the same man who had been cured of that infirmity was likewise brought out from the people, and was seen walking on his own feet, to the great joy of the whole Church, attesting the proclamations of divine praise by certain tangible proofs, the healed and sound limbs of his own body. So while these things were being done, and while at one and the same time the facts themselves wonderfully came together in harmonious unity with each thing written, you would surely have thought that past things were not so much being narrated as present things being shown. For what was uttered in speech was at once seen in the present work itself, so that the miracles themselves were made more wonderful by another, greater miracle. Who was so hard and iron as not to burst into tears? not to melt into devotion and humility? Who could ever speak of it with fitting praise? A cry of rejoicing arose at the hearing of the reading; and again a greater exultation was stirred at the beholding of the sight; and so through hearing and seeing the flame of divine love then pierced every human heart. These things I could not pass over in silence, for the sake of renewing the memory of those who were present at that time, and so as by no means to cheat of knowledge those to whom these things were hidden; and because those very things that were read out were at once also taken down and copied by very many devout people together with their closing passage, for that reason, with the Lord's help, we have made from here a beginning, as it were, of a second little book, for narrating the other things that followed. I will relate to you, therefore, dearly beloved, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, further wonders of a deed done by Stephen, our common patron, a memorable story well known to many, to the praise and glory of God.
CHAPTER II. — On Megetia, who had been struck with paralysis, who had failed in the hands of the physicians, and, running to Saint Stephen, was cured of a double infirmity.

1. There was a certain woman of the city of Carthage, noble in birth, nobler in the faith of Christ, Megetia by name, rich in the world, richer in God; her mother, a Christian, was named Vitula, but her husband, father-in-law and father were pagans. When she had [a child] in her womb, in the fourth month of her conception, first from nausea and vomiting, from what cause I do not know, while she suffered quite frequently upheaval of the stomach, gaping of the mouth and provocation of vomiting, her case was brought to the deformity and plague of paralysis, so that, the very hinges of the teeth and the joints being forced from their places, she could by no means close her slackened mouth, nor have free and sound movements of palate and tongue either to send anything out of the mouth or to take anything into it. There remained in this devout and modest woman a misshapen and repellent appearance, and the stain of the defect was fixed on her body in the very place where it could by no means be hidden: for it was the face, of which someone had said, The brow displays the person, which cannot be covered without disgrace. For when the functions of the other limbs are hindered by some defect, some are withdrawn from shame by care. But when the face itself has been disfigured by some ugliness, whatever covering is applied for modesty's sake only increases the shame itself. What then was the noble matron to do, hiding her damaged mouth with a veil, when the fellowship and courtesy of life itself compelled her either to give a kiss or to converse with other noble women likewise coming to greet her, to say nothing of food and drink, which she could barely and with difficulty eat or swallow? For the skill and diligence of the physicians, labouring long and much over her in vain, not only could bring her no health, but the case even went on for the worse. And not without reason: for she was not yet being reshaped by God, the founder and redeemer of all nature, as nothing is formed except by his power, by whose judgement and discipline every human body is bound, and by whose medicine it is loosed. Worn out, therefore, by such sorrow and pain, and helped by no relief from any remedies or medicines, by now almost in the sixth month, the body and spirit of the delicate young woman had wasted away. Because of this, she also kept within the enclosure of her womb, dead, what she was carrying, already deprived of the breath of life. Thus, when before, under the single defect of paralysis, life itself was already dreadful, another graver and more dangerous thing was added, from which not even the very possibility of living would remain. For if the young woman had so failed under the trouble of her damaged mouth, how could she live with the collapse of a dead womb? The seventh month had come; neither was the face stripped of its baneful deformity, nor was the belly stripped of its dead burden. But Pontius, Megetia's father, and her father-in-law Avitianus, and her husband Adventius, being still bound by the errors of paganism, toiled altogether vainly and emptily at whatever they could attempt, as if for the life of the dying Megetia, not only through the skill of physicians but also through the arts of demons and the fictions of superstitious vanities. But, unhappy error, why did you believe you could confer human health, which you have always striven to take away? The voice of truth refutes you in the most holy Psalms, testifying generally and briefly from whom truly comes all health of soul and body, saying: Salvation is the Lord's (Ps. 3:9). For to God alone is it rightly sung, Men and beasts you will save, O Lord (Ps. 35:7). He who deigned to create, he indeed deigned also to heal.

2. So, while those persons just mentioned had long laboured vainly at such things, and were drowsing not in body but in heart, behold, God, that teacher who neither slumbers nor sleeps, who keeps Israel (Ps. 120:4); that same God, I say, who has care for all (Wis. 6:8), kindled the devout Vitula, Megetia's mother, with the warmth of faith, and inspired her to run to the aid of his Friend, the lord Stephen. When this blessed woman set out from the city of Carthage to that of Uzalis, to the place of the holy relics, the most merciful and compassionate Lord received her, heard her, helped her, and granted her what she sought for her daughter, and let her triumph as victor over the defeated devil, the adversary. It cannot be told with what tearful cries that devout woman approached the Friend of God, and with what pity, prostrate before the threshold of the glorious Martyr, she poured out the griefs of her heart, breaking into these words: "Lord Stephen, friend of Christ, help a wretched mother who flees to you for the safety of her endangered daughter. Here, then, I entreat you with laments; there, I implore, may your handmaid feel you as a present physician. You yourself know with what troubles Megetia labours, and in what peril of life she is placed. See for how long she has lain, wretched in her whole body, both undone by paralysis and wasted in her womb. And it is near that, the seventh month completed, she will be overtaken by the eighth. All despair of Megetia's recovery; I, who have fled to Christ and to you, his Friend, believe that such mourning for my daughter will not be laid upon my head. I ask and pray that, when I return from here, from your crown, and begin to hasten to your handmaid, my soul may be refreshed by some good news of my daughter." When with these and many similar addresses she seemed to herself to have sufficiently instructed Saint Stephen as advocate before Christ the judge, the mother, in travail of heart, returned in haste to see again her daughter, her one and only greatest care. Yet she brought back with her from the shrine of the blessed Martyr sanctified oil, and a cloth or napkin, a witness to her prayers and her sweat for the health of her suffering daughter. And behold, on the way, when she had withdrawn to avoid the heat (for it was summer, when the fiery sun was scorching the earth), a messenger suddenly arrived and she received a letter sent from Carthage by her husband, just as she had asked in her prayers, in which the imminent deliverance of her daughter was indicated. For it said that her daughter would enter the eighth month the next day, yet was somewhat livelier, and that signs of her delivery were already appearing, and that she should be of good heart about her daughter. All of this was announced to the devout mother Vitula not by a human mouth but by a divine oracle. Relieved, then, by these first auspices of her prayers, the mother flew there swiftly. When she reached Carthage and found her child placed at the very turning-point of her life, she at once anointed her daughter's limbs with the sacred oil, and also gave her the napkin to clasp to her breast. When this was done, Megetia came back to life, freed of the burden of her womb, and, having entered the days of the eighth month that pregnant women dread, was restored from the very palace of death to the air of the living. And so, one deadly affliction having been settled, there remained another for the heavenly chief physician to cure at once. That this might come about without delay, the faithful mother Vitula wished to bring her freed daughter back with her to the vein of the life-giving spring from which she had brought the heavenly draught to her sick one and had poured it in to her health. But Megetia's strength, not yet recovered after the toil of her dangerous delivery, by no means allowed her to undertake the further toil of the journey.

3. Meanwhile the young woman's husband, father-in-law and father, still in no way moved to the praise of God and of his true first Martyr by so pitiable an affliction of the womb, began again, in order to cure her remaining ailment, that is, the deformity of her damaged mouth, to consult those human remedies and errors, and to wear away long stretches of time in vain. For a whole year and some months more had passed thus. At length the faithful mother Vitula summoned to herself a certain chief physician of the city of Carthage, named Felix, most trustworthy above the rest and a friend of her house, and bound him by an oath on the life of his only daughter, saying: "As your only daughter may live: can Megetia be cured of this paralysis, or not?" Then he said: "I tell you truly, since you have chosen to bind me so, that your daughter cannot be fully cured of this affliction. The joint itself," he said, "like that of a cart, where certain fastenings of the mouth and jaws are held, has been forced out of its place." Mother Vitula, grounded in the steadfastness of her faith, at once answered him, saying: "I do not believe so in my Christ, that my daughter will be left thus in so great an evil of paralysis." And he, greatly marvelling at the firmness of faith in a woman, said: "This the almighty God in whom you believe may do; but hope for nothing from us." Having heard this, the devout Vitula sent the physician away, took her Megetia with her, went to her husband and her daughter's husband, and, inflamed with holy grief, began to speak thus: "We have wretchedly given in to you until now," she said, "nor could we women resist [you] men; long have we endured your wishes, from which no fruit, no effect for our daughter's health has come, so that, behold, for a year and the further months that run on, my daughter's body has only been wearied in the hands of physicians, and, as you see, has not been healed at all by anything they achieve. I beg you, allow us at last, too, to do what is good for us: let us also go to our physician. I believe in him, that he who did not wish Megetia to die with her dead child will also make her live among people with her face healed." When these just and true complaints and others of this kind had been tearfully uttered, those men could in no way resist such a woman, clothed with a manly spirit. They preferred to yield of their own accord rather than to depart defeated by the judgement of someone else.

4. So when they had been brought round to this view of mother Vitula, that is, Megetia's husband and likewise her father, the husband indeed still a pagan, but the father now made a Christian catechumen, Pontius by name, a man of senatorial rank (it is fitting that, as we have begun to declare his faith in Christ, we should now also begin to name him with due honour; and how indeed he was initiated into the Christian name, since the place seems to require it, it will not irk us to disclose. For when the devout Vitula, before Megetia had been freed from the danger of childbirth, had set out to the Friend of God, there in her prayers she had also pleaded for the belief of this venerable husband of hers, that he might be imbued with the Christian faith and name. And this was revealed to her that very night in the following vision. She seemed to see beside the shrine of the blessed Martyr two shining candlesticks, both blazing alike with fire, and Pontius, her husband already mentioned, seemed to stand there with her and appear, and to say to her: "Vitula, our candlestick shines better; and so I want you to know that I have now laid down my necks." Having seen and heard this, the devout Vitula awoke from sleep, and in the morning, when prayer was completed, began to recount to certain handmaids of God what she had seen in her sleep. And she herself first interpreted her dream, saying to those virgins standing round: "Let Your Holiness know that Pontius will soon believe in Christ, as I trust in my Christ. For this is what he signified to me in the dream, saying: 'I want you to know, Vitula, that I have now laid down my necks', surely only under the yoke of Christ." Thus, then, the honourable Pontius was made, as I said, first a Christian catechumen in the following year, on the same days on which the blessed Stephen had been entreated by the devout Vitula for her husband's eternal salvation).

5. But, as I had begun to say, with their men consenting, mother Vitula and her Megetia set out together from Carthage and came together to the shrine of the blessed Martyr, and then, prostrate before his sacred threshold, weeping and wailing day and night, squalid in ashes and sackcloth, noble women not blushing before people so that they might be pleasing to God, they took up what is sung in the Psalms: My tears have been my bread day and night, while it is said to me daily, Where is your God? (Ps. 41:4). For these devout and noble women did not lack taunts from unbelievers about our very Christian religion, which they recalled before the Lord with tearful cries and, as it is written, with bitter words, and poured out their soul upon themselves. For it was said by the enemies of our faith: "Where is your God?" So mother Vitula cried out into the ears of the Friend of God: "Lord Stephen, behold, I have brought to you your Megetia, whom you yourself freed from death. Nor did you let us become a joy to the enemy, not handing us over to the will of those who afflict us, who disparage and despair of Christ our Lord and of you, so great a Friend of his. Make them, I pray, make them blush again at the whole and full health of your Megetia, as you have already made them blush at the most dangerous trouble of her womb. You will surely not fail in lesser things, who have granted greater. What I promised her pagan husband about you, fulfil for your own sake. Let not the mother be put to shame in her daughter, she who presumed upon you, who fled to you. Surely, that the eye of the heart of those who do not yet believe and who mock us may be healed, let my daughter's mouth be cured; and that health of soul may be gained for them, let the girl be granted health of her limbs."

6. When tearful words of this kind and in this sense had been poured out, the seventh day had passed, when behold, in the dead of night Megetia was visited in her sleep: she saw a man of distinguished appearance appear to her, wearing the dress of a deacon. She began to ask him, as if he were a kind of spiritual physician, to examine her mouth and, if he would deign to, to cure it. But as soon as he had examined her mouth, he looked at her with a cheerful face and a serene gaze and said: "Indeed your mouth is not yet straight; but look up, and see what is flying above your head." At once she raised her eyes above her and saw a most hideous serpent flying above her with the oars of its wings, and wandering this way and that in twisting coils. But Megetia, terrified at the horrible and monstrous sight, was strengthened by the exhortation of that distinguished man, who said to her: "Unless you first kill this serpent, you cannot be healed. But do not be afraid; engage with it with a brave spirit, and you will overcome entirely." Hearing this, Megetia, armed with the strength of her faith and the protection of so great a helper, seized what seemed a rod offered to her at that moment and fought against that most hideous and most twisting dragon. Though she was long exercised and long wearied by the resisting adversary, yet at last, when she struck it on the head, she laid it low at once. Awakened in fearful joy at this, she leapt from her bed and was fully awake. And when she pondered what the meaning of her dream portended and could not understand it clearly, she then prayed to be visited [again] and asked to be strengthened, and then gave herself up to rest. Behold, she saw again that young man, comely in dress, shining in a snow-white garment, and at once, as if he stretched out his hand to her as she lay, she heard him command and say: "Arise, thus you are cured." But Megetia, as she had been accustomed to do before for a human physician, turned her head towards him and offered him her mouth as if to be treated. But he, as if correcting the act of one who did not understand, answered her: "Why do you do this? First your eyes must be cured." She replied, saying: "My lord, I have healthy eyes, but I ask you to cure my mouth." And he said: "I have already told you, first the eyes in you must be cured." Then, like a heavenly chief physician, looking into the secrets of the heart by the Spirit, he put on a salve as if a medicinal [one] on the skin, anointed her eyes, and departed. Now when in the morning the devout Megetia told this dream of hers to her dearest and most holy women, in the very course of her account she was spontaneously pricked in heart and suddenly stung by the memory of a certain sin of hers, and did not delay to confess her sin, but, as it is written, she acknowledged her offence and did not cover her unrighteousness (Psalm 31:5). Behold, then, which were the eyes that had first to be cured in her: not those of the body, but of the heart, which, as a [true physician], the glorious Stephen declared, [saying]: "First your eyes must be cured." For what lay hidden and faulty in the mind had to be healed, so that thus at last what was seen to be deformed in the body might be healed. Hence also that most hideous serpent which was flying above her head, because it held the ruling mind of the rational soul, had to be crushed and conquered. For when the guilt of any offence is humbly acknowledged, the head of the snake is shattered by penitence, and the eye of the heart is cleansed by confession. So on the twelfth day from when she had come with her mother to the Friend of God, while she was praying at the place of the sacred shrine, knocking with the devotion of faith not only with the affection of her heart but also with the movement of her body, she pushed and opened the very little doors of the shrine and, doing violence to the kingdom of God, put her head inside and pressed it upon the resting-place of the holy relics, and washed and watered everything there with her tears. And behold, by the mercy from above of him who draws near to the contrite of heart (Psalm 146), Megetia the handmaid of God felt her mouth being straightened and stroked by a hand, as it were visible and tangible. After she rose from prayer, she told this, trembling and rejoicing, to the choirs of holy virgins standing round, who were saying praises to God there for her and with her. What and how great joy there was then in all minds, and what feeling of weeping it stirred up before God himself, can scarcely be told.

7. But before we come to the most longed-for end of the affair, where we shall show the full and perfect health of the devout Megetia, cured and helped by the Friend of God in the name of Christ, we must by no means pass over another thing that happened wonderfully in the midst of this. When mother and daughter had persisted in prayer about the place of the holy Martyr for nearly forty days, behold, suddenly a letter came, sent to them at Carthage, in which the girl's father, the honourable Pontius, was said to be ill in body, and they set out from the city of Uzalis to visit him. But when, midway on the journey, because of the heat, they wished to use the baths to refresh the body, there was present a certain servant woman who knew Megetia, sent to meet them by the unbeliever, not so much to greet as rather to spy. Since she was eager, more curiously than was proper, to see the bare mouth and face of the blessed Megetia, she went in with her to attend her, and when she had looked as much as she wished at the face of the handmaid of God, she saw Megetia's mouth appearing to her entirely whole and sound. At this sight that servant, astonished and amazed, since she had found other than she expected, at once turned to a certain consecrated virgin standing beside her and, addressing her by name, said: "Child Helpidiana, the lady Megetia is entirely healed." For thus the grace of God was strong in Megetia, that, although the fuller cure in her body was in some part deferred, yet the perfect appearance of health was set before the eyes of the unbelievers to strike them back. And that handmaid of God, understanding the great mystery of God, answered that poor woman, saying: "Unbelievers, believe at least now."

8. Again, at Carthage, when one day the blessed Megetia was talking with her pagan husband, and in the course of conversation she appeared to her husband with a whole mouth and face, her husband, moved by this sight, began to rejoice and say: "Lady Megetia, I see you entirely healed." But she, for the time hiding by pretence what the divine power was showing in her, kept to the course of her talk. And he likewise could not keep silent about what he saw, and as before he said to her: "You are entirely healed, thanks be to God." And she, filled with joy, at last smiling, said to her husband: "Will you at least now believe in Christ?" And he said: "What do you want me to do about my father? For I too want to become a Christian."

9. But, to come now to the end we promised: the most holy day of Easter was approaching, and behold, the blessed Megetia was asked by a friend, a noble woman Rustica, to go with her to the blessed martyr Cyprian at Mappalia to fulfil her vow, and to take part with her in the festival. Megetia pleaded that she could not do this, knowing what the power of God was showing in her to the eyes of unbelievers, and what of full health heavenly grace was still holding in reserve. Yet, not wishing to grieve her friend, she did not refuse outright, but promised that on that day she would certainly do what God willed. But when that friend had gone, Megetia did not cease to persist in prayer day and night. Every day she first took a morsel dipped in sanctified oil, and so took her other food. Then one night she was visited in her sleep, so that she thought she was standing beside the shrine of the blessed Stephen and saw there that handsome young man, suffused with bright light and borne on a splendid horse, with very many shining lamps and a most splendid procession going before him, and it was said to her by him in a clear voice: "This light belongs to you, Megetia; receive it." After this vision she awoke filled with joy, and as soon as she felt herself healed, she put her hands to her mouth and face to examine them, and, as if through excessive joy not trusting herself alone, she woke her maidservants who were resting around her bed with a loud voice and called them to run to her to look at and gaze upon her. Then they, when they saw that the gift of God had been fulfilled in their lady and that the prayer of all had been accomplished, all cried out together in gladness and burst into the praise of God. The day appointed for her by her friend also arrived; people came from various quarters to the devout Megetia, asking that, as she had promised, she would deign to go to the appointed place and not desert her dear ones. But Megetia, the handmaid of God, with her mouth still covered with a veil, as was her custom, came out from her inner chamber to her friends. When she had let them be sad about her for some time, she suddenly took the veil from her face, and showing her face, said: "Behold, see what God has deigned to accomplish in me, and rejoice with me, and give thanks to the Lord himself for me." When all saw her, rejoicing and blessing the Lord, they began to cover her with kisses and to embrace her. Then all went together with her to the church and paid their vows to the Lord. And when the holy Easter of the Lord was over, the devout Vitula, together with her Megetia and other devout women, came also to the city of Uzalis, and joyfully rendered, fervently offered, and fruitfully paid her vows for her daughter's full and perfect health to Christ the Lord and to the Friend of Christ, in the sight of our whole Church rejoicing and congratulating with her.

CHAPTER III. — A certain Donatus, who had a wine-store, found almost two hundred jars of wine spoiled; at his order a servant brought a flagon filled from all the jars, and running to Saint Stephen and placing it there, he prayed; and returning with the flagon, he poured some of it into all the jars, and the wine was restored.

There is said to be a certain man, Donatus, father of a son who was also most honourable, named Rusticus, an accountant of the prefects, very well known to all. On his suburban estate, called by the name of its place, he used to lay down and keep wines of good quality every year. Meanwhile, as is the custom of landowners, for the sake of profitable gain, to prefer to offer whatever produce of the land they have stored for sale to buyers at the moment when the prices of the season run higher, in line with their wishes for the profits they long for, it seemed good to the said master of the estate to go first into his wine-store with a certain man of his, a most expert taster of wine, and to approve the wines by examining them jar by jar. When this was done, as soon as the taster put the wine drawn from a jar to the judgement of his lips, at once the man's astonished mouth and face turned pale. For besides the fact that the wine's most foul colour offered of itself a sight for the eyes to turn from, its most dismal savour also forced on the lips a taste to grieve at. But since this evil was thought to lie in one jar only, the loss was not held to be so troublesome a damage to the householder. But when they began to go round jar by jar, and the whole number of the jars, that is, nearly two hundred, was examined and found to have likewise degenerated and perished, what the owner's feelings were there at that moment, what the grief of the store-keeper himself, I think no compassionate human heart can fail to know. For indeed no small and contemptible loss or damage had befallen, but nearly two hundred jars, as I said, which were thought to be completely full of the sweetest wine, were on the contrary found filled with the filth not even of vinegar, but of some most corrupt and dreg-laden liquid. What was the master of his ruined property to do, having suffered the destruction of his vintage not still on the vines, but, what is more grievous, in the wine-store itself? What, I say, was he to do? What could he have done with wine so corrupt and no longer to be called wine? Should he perhaps have sold it at some utterly worthless price? But what buyer would be so foolish as to approach so worthless a thing? Should he at least pour it out and throw it away? But who would so forget his own labours as readily to expose the produce of a whole year, such as it was, to be trampled by men and beasts? At last his soul, tossing in such griefs, breathed upon by the breeze of divine inspiration, was brought by grace, as by sail, into the most faithful harbour and the safest anchorage. For as he turned many things over within himself, this better resolve settled in the owner's mind: that he must take refuge with the Friend of God, Saint Stephen, the first martyr of Christ. So he ordered that taster of his wine to fill one small flask from any one of his jars, to carry it at dawn to the shrine of the Blessed one to be blessed, and from there at once to bring it back sanctified, and then to pour a little of it over into all the jars and go away. O Lord, Lord, who have care for man, doing all things kindly for man's sake, who once through your saints healed bitter and barren waters by casting in wood and throwing in a vessel of salt (Exod. 15:25; 4 Kgs 2:21), and through yourself, Lord, turned water into wine (John 2:1-11), you yourself now, through your friend Saint Stephen too, have restored ruined wines to their former state, turning bitterness into sweetness, blackness into brightness, grief into exultation! So that faithful servant quickly carried out his master's orders: he drew the flagon as he had been told, went, set it down, brought it back, gave a very little to each jar, and went away. On the next day, mindful of his faith and of his order, the householder rose early, met the servant who knew of the task, and led him along with him as his companion to the wine-store: all the jars are inspected again in order; the wine is drawn, brightness is seen in the colour, the savour is approved in the taste, sadness is changed into joy, and it is found how much and how greatly faith in Christ and in his most glorious Friend avails, and the news passes on to all who hear and marvel; finally, those most excellent wines are distributed to buyers at a fitting price. See how divine providence serves the needs of men: and what, then, is offered or rendered to God for such great benefits of his?

CHAPTER IV. — Where a great dragon appeared from the sky, at the sight of which all the people fled to the threshold of Stephen, and as they prayed it was gradually withdrawn among the fleeces of the clouds and was seen no more.

1. One day a market was being held in our city, and when it was already midday the clear face of the sky was suddenly stirred into a foul and murky turbulence of the air. And behold, above there was seen a fiery dragon of immense size, hanging head downward from the clouds. This ought not to seem so unusual and new, not only because of common knowledge, but also because of the authority of holy Scripture, which speaks of dragons thus: "Praise the Lord from the earth, dragons and all deeps, fire, hail, snow, ice, stormy wind, which do his word" (Ps. 148:7-8). [For the] deep [...] is not only the depth of the waters here below, but also, above, the immensity [of the air] which we look up to, which seems to grow thick with moisture: when [...] breezes are stirred up, [clouds are gathered] like fleeces of wool, fiery lightnings are sent forth. [Lest] all these things, as the foolishly wise suppose, should be believed to happen by chance and fortune, holy Scripture watchfully provided: and after it said, "Fire, hail, snow, ice, stormy wind", it at once added, concerning the very Creator and Ruler of the universe, "which do his word". So then, the dragon hanging, as I said, by this providence of God's ordering, and blazing among the clouds, as if coming forth and flashing out of the upper deep, when the moving air carried it hither and thither for some time, and the trembling of all who were present, waiting and stunned, saw that it was about to plunge at any moment on the middle of the city, the common crowd began to flee from the public gathering, and ran about everywhere, wherever fear drove them, as each one could. In short, the whole market itself was broken up and thrown into confusion. For abandoning all earthly business, people feared for their life alone. For who then would seek profits of money, bewailing in so great a peril the losses of the soul? Or who would think even of food for the body, dreading the final setting of his life? Who, further, would desire clothing, losing his mind for fear of death? A great concourse of the multitude also flew straightway to the bosom of Mother Church, to the mercy of God the Father. At the very consecrated shrine of the Friend of God lay, prostrate on their faces, every age and both sexes. At last, when prayer had been poured out fittingly to Christ by the lord Stephen on behalf of the tears of all, with the consent of God's clemency, that horrible dragon began gradually to be withdrawn from the sight of men among the enclosures of the clouds and hidden, and, where the winds had pressed down, as the clear face of the sky returned, to be scattered and driven off; and so, their spirits being restored and brought back from such great sadness to joy, abundant thanks were rendered to God and to his Friend, with great tears poured out from this unexpected rejoicing.

2. To this is added also something else more wonderful than this very miracle: so that human frailty, ignorant in all things, should not, being taught nothing more clearly and openly about the divine judgements and benefits, have failed to be grateful as was fitting. For behold, on the next day, by the arrangement of divine providence, a certain merchant never known to our region came of his own accord to our subdeacon named Sennodus at the place Memblotutanum, called him to himself, and asked him who he was and where from. When he said he was a subdeacon of the Church of Uzalis, that unknown man (if indeed only a man: for it is to be believed that he was an angel and a man; for it is neither unheard of nor untried, whether for the Christian religion or for human knowledge, that holy Angels have often appeared to men in earthly dress and visible form) at once answered. He gave, then, to the said subdeacon a cloth painted in various colours, on which was this picture: on the right side of the cloth Saint Stephen himself was seen standing, and carrying the glorious cross laid on his own shoulders, with the point of which cross he was seen to knock at the gate of a city, out of which a most foul dragon was seen to come forth fleeing, namely at the coming of the Friend of God. But that harmful serpent, not at all safe even in its flight, was seen crushed and pressed beneath the triumphant foot of Christ's Martyr. When, then, this picture on the cloth, not at all without a mystery of God, had been brought by the said subdeacon and likewise hung up before the very shrine of so great a patron, every age and every sex began to gaze and marvel, as at a great spectacle, by what author, that is, or by what deliverer that dragon had been destroyed and the enemy overcome. For the testimony of the following [day] commended to the minds of all the truth of what had been done on the previous day. For what was looked at more attentively in the cloth [...] was [proved] more credibly in reality. [...] concurred with [...], and what had been done by divine power the day before [...] was recalled as much as it was afterwards [...] in [...]. In short, from this very agreement [of the preceding] and the following truth, and from the image [...] of certain copies, so great love, admiration and rejoicing were kindled in [...] alike, that nothing else at all was said or affirmed by everyone but this one thing: "Truly God through his Friend has delivered this city, and has driven a great plague from us." And indeed it was a kind of address of God to men, [...] in the cloth, silently signifying, as it were, and saying: "O wretched mortals, from what a fire of the dragon you escaped yesterday, and whose intercession, as your advocate, was accepted for you, understand from the figure of this cloth on this following day, and rejoice. Hence compare among yourselves both your preceding trial and your subsequent deliverance, and then, not doubting but certain, give thanks to your God through my Friend. Behold, you see the dragon put to flight and driven out of your city; behold my first Martyr crushing its head; behold the trophy of the Cross, through which you have conquered the enemy." In this way, then, our city having first been delivered from so great a danger, and afterwards instructed and enlightened by such an admonition through the fitting picture on the cloth, every devout soul was gladdened by a twofold miracle in the glory of God.
CHAPTER V. — On the steward of the public money of Carthage, who was delivered.

1. In the miracles told above of the lord Stephen, our common patron, we remember that we have set out, as far as our modest ability allowed, mighty works of healing and visions in dreams and what they brought about. Now, with the Lord's help, we wish to tell of bodily appearances and manifestations made by the Friend of God himself, plainly and yet with the faith concealed under human dress: in the forum, in the courts, in the light of day, in the gathering of the people, before men of rank and office, to people awake and watching. So then, the steward of the public money of the city of Carthage, named Florentius, as commonly happens to those who conduct fiscal business in such offices, that they often provoke the anger of the authorities under whom they live and whose power they serve, had himself incurred the displeasure of judicial indignation to the point of danger to his life. For this reason, by an order of the proconsul, from what cause I do not know, he was commanded to be seized in haste and brought at once before his eyes. When the office staff, which was obeying [the order], had carried this out without any delay, and had seized the said steward, brought him through the streets, and presented him to the proconsul as he sat in the inner chamber, at once a great pallor began to spread through the hearts of those who were present and looking on, and who grieved for the man with human pity and feared for his danger.
