Meanwhile, as soon as he saw the man he had been seeking in fury, the angry authority rose up with a terrible voice, alarming the steward with a threatening interrogation. But the terrified man's mind fled from fear, and he could not find anything to say. But behold, God, that master who looks down from heaven upon the children of men, mixing mildness with severity, turning threats into kindness, loving in chastising, consoling in loving, a judge in his scourges, a father in his caresses, everywhere faithful, nowhere cruel, this God and Lord sent his angel to deliver the man, of whom it is said: "The angel of the Lord will send [help] round about those who fear him, and will rescue them" (Ps. 33:8). For when that steward, uncertain and in doubt of his life, stood among the interrogators in such great fear of the terrible authority, he suddenly felt himself struck from behind. At once, with his neck bowed a little and his eyes turned stealthily backwards, he saw what seemed one of the executioners standing beside him, prompting him what to do and whom he ought to entreat, and saying and urging: "Call upon Saint Stephen." Having seen and heard this, Florentius, restored to his mind and senses, and strengthened in spirit that had just now been revived from its flight, did not cease to pray to and call upon the glorious Stephen within himself. Then, lifting his face a little towards the judge who was questioning him, he fixed his eyes on the judge's assessor. He saw him shining and gleaming with a new face and a new countenance, and perceived that it was not the man he knew very well, but another, unknown and wonderful counsellor of the judge; for while the assessor had previously been known to everyone for the ugliness of a face withered by age and for his old years, in the one who appeared to him there shone the beauty and brightness of a youthful countenance. Having seen this, the said Florentius, long and greatly moved, no longer doubting but firm and certain, believed that the glorious Stephen was there present, that from a hidden seat he was attending to him, and that in his case he was sitting as judge or assisting the judge. For so that he might take confidence more fully and completely from such a vision and presence of the Friend of God, Florentius saw this same advocate of his, and most merciful counsellor in his trial, also nodding to him with his hand, signalling with his right hand that he should fear nothing at all, smiling at him with a cheerful face, and promising him the fullest hope of safety. In short: little by little those furious impulses of the judge and his swelling temper began to be brought down to complete calm and mildness, so that [Florentius] did not dread a judge but recognised a father, and did not fear his axe for his own head but hoped for his favour for his own safety. O Lord, Lord, who command your true praises to be sung to you in the sacred psalms, not out of arrogance but out of mercy, not for your boasting but for our protection, when it is said: "You rule the power of the sea, and you calm the motion of its waves" (Ps. 88:10)! With this the authority of the Gospel also agrees, where, when at the command of your Christ the turbulent waves and winds were smoothed, the disciples said in wonder: "What kind of man is this, who commands the winds and the sea, and they obey him?" (Luke 8:25). And most true is what is also said of you elsewhere in the words of sacred Scripture: "The heart of the king is in the hand of the Lord, like running water; wherever he wills, there he turns it" (Prov. 21:1). For you, Lord, through the consular authority, first angry and afterwards calmed towards the steward, showed in our times what you showed long ago, in the authority of ancient Scripture, concerning the holy woman Esther, through a royal authority first raging and then again caressing, and which you gave to posterity to be read and known as a memorial (Esther 15). Accordingly the proconsul, with the executioners sent away, not only ordered the steward Florentius, no longer as his official but as a son, to come close to him, even to his bosom, without any fear, but also began to admonish him more familiarly with fatherly affection, and then, granting him pardon and sparing his life, let him leave the inner chamber a free man. When this was done, those who stood by and had trembled with devout anxiety for the man's danger, as the steward went away acquitted and unharmed, with joy mixed with amazement now hesitated, now exulted, now, wondering and inquiring among themselves, said: "Where does this so sudden change and reversal of affairs come from, which has stripped the proconsular authority of all severity and brought it to such humanity and mildness that it has led a man back to life from the very threshold of death?"

2. Florentius, moreover, though the danger was past, returned home still somewhat wounded in spirit by his earlier fear. Indeed, he did not at the time confess to any of his household what had happened, what he had seen, what he had escaped. But that same night, in a dream, he saw appear to him the one he had seen in the inner chamber, clothed in youthful form, [on the] threshold, and heard himself addressed by name unprompted: "What is it, Florentius? Do you recognise me? I am the one who appeared to you in the inner chamber and delivered you from death." When Florentius recognised him and understood that he was Stephen, and wished to worship him, he was raised up by him with a hand placed under his chin. On waking, Florentius rose early in the morning and, desiring to pay his thanks to God and to fulfil his vows to his Friend, set out alone for the city of Uzalis. But since the roads were unknown to him, the ignorant traveller prayed silently within himself and implored the guidance of that same glorious Martyr of Christ. And while he was pouring out his prayer, behold, in the silence of his praying, a presbyter of our church, named Firmus, came up from elsewhere and joined Florentius. Seeing him, Florentius asked him where he was travelling. The said presbyter replied that he was going to the city of Uzalis, and also declared that he was a presbyter from there. Then Florentius, gladdened in spirit, began to rejoice greatly; he could not hide all his joy, but from the very beginning of the affair he related in order to the aforesaid presbyter, who had joined him as companion of his journey, what the divine mercy had done for him through its glorious Friend. Then, the journey ended, Florentius came to the city together with the presbyter, entered the threshold of the blessed Martyr with humble devotion, and, prostrate on the pavement, gave thanks to the almighty Lord Jesus Christ and to his most blessed Friend. Entering the monasteries too, he related all this to the venerable bishop and at the same time to the company of the servants of God that came running to him. And he eagerly roused us also, and most fervently kindled us, together with himself, with much thanksgiving to the praises of God and of the crown of the martyr Stephen. These things, few out of many, have been told by us, as far as the pen was able to search them out, and to commend them to devout hearts to be read with longing rather than with distaste.
